title: Livin The Dream

jokes.text: Jim takes time off from Philly work to be with Pam, describing phone ringing off the hook, then pivoting to 'This does. It's the only thing that matters.' followed by 'Nice morning, too. Beesly. Oh, my God.'
jokes.setup: Jim delivers a sincere talking-head about stepping back from his Philly ambitions to focus on his marriage, building emotional sincerity
jokes.punchline: 'Nice morning, too. Beesly. Oh, my God.' — the sudden drop into smitten, goofy husband mode undercuts the gravity with pure warmth and comedy
jokes.explanation: Works because it earns the warmth through context — we know Jim's been neglecting Pam. The sudden shift to lovestruck goofiness is character-specific and sweet-funny.

jokes.text: Andy asks Erin: 'Which tie makes me look like a guy who likes sofas? My agent's putting me up for a furniture commercial.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks for fashion advice in a seemingly normal workplace moment
jokes.punchline: The reason is a furniture commercial — he needs to 'look like a guy who likes sofas,' a perfectly absurd and specific qualifier
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a guy who likes sofas' is genuinely funny — it's the kind of absurd actor-brain logic that is perfectly Andy. Economy is excellent; the joke lands in one sentence.

jokes.text: Pete greets Jim: 'So, Big Tuna, what's up? Back in the small pond?' Jim: 'For now, yeah.' Pete: 'Thin-sliced Tuna. Carpaccio. Go on.'
jokes.setup: Pete uses Jim's old nickname 'Big Tuna' and the 'big pond/small pond' idiom
jokes.punchline: 'Thin-sliced Tuna. Carpaccio.' — Pete riffs on the tuna metaphor with escalating culinary specificity
jokes.explanation: A fun bit of wordplay that shows Pete trying to bond with Jim. 'Carpaccio' is a nice escalation. Slightly undercut by Pete not being a deeply established character.

jokes.text: Andy tells Jim: 'Half the time, I don't know if I'm wearing my stage makeup or my work makeup.'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining that he can't give 100% to both acting and managing
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Andy wears two distinct categories of makeup — stage AND work — implies he wears makeup to the office as a matter of course
jokes.explanation: High character integration — only Andy would have both categories of makeup and not see anything unusual about it. The implication lands as a perfect absurdist character beat without needing elaboration.

jokes.text: Oscar asks Angela 'Is everything okay?' Angela flatly replies: 'No. Everything is not okay.'
jokes.setup: Oscar asks the standard pleasantry question
jokes.punchline: Angela's completely unfiltered, blunt refusal to offer social niceties — delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Functional Angela character beat. Works because of her established bluntness but isn't particularly original — this type of Angela response is a known quantity.

jokes.text: Angela reveals: 'The county took my cats... Two sacks' worth. Apparently, my apartment complex has rules about how many pets are too many for a studio.'
jokes.setup: Angela says the county took her cats
jokes.punchline: 'Two sacks' worth' — the casual unit of measurement for cats, and the implication that she was storing cats in sacks (or removing them required sacks), combined with the reveal she had so many that even her studio apartment rules were triggered
jokes.explanation: 'Two sacks' worth' is a brilliantly weird unit. Angela's cat hoarding has always been a running gag, but 'sacks' escalates it to a dark-comic place. High character integration — this is peak Angela behavior described in peak Angela vocabulary.

jokes.text: Angela describes her downstairs neighbor as 'this uptight, judgmental shrew. You know the type.' Oscar, directly to camera, deadpans: 'I've never met anyone like that.'
jokes.setup: Angela describes her neighbor as an uptight, judgmental shrew — the exact description that fits Angela herself
jokes.punchline: Oscar's talking-head deadpan to camera: 'I've never met anyone like that' — obvious irony since Angela is literally that type
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is clean and well-executed: the irony is sharp, Oscar's camera look sells it, and the economy ('I've never met anyone like that') is excellent. The audience is ahead of the joke which makes it satisfying rather than cheap.

jokes.text: Angela says 'Without my cats, I am utterly and completely alone.' Oscar gently notes: 'Angela, you still have your son.' Angela replies: 'I guess.'
jokes.setup: Angela laments being utterly alone without her cats
jokes.punchline: When reminded she has a child, she offers only 'I guess' — treating her son as a distant afterthought compared to her cats
jokes.explanation: Perfectly dark. 'I guess' is the exact right amount of reluctant acknowledgment — it doesn't over-explain the joke. Angela ranking her cats above her child is an extreme extension of her established character that pays off beautifully in one word.

jokes.text: Dwight announces his knuckles are 'four new deadly weapons' named 'Basher, Thrasher, Crasher and...' then pauses. Kevin volunteers: 'Smasher?' Dwight: 'Smasher? No. Where'd you get that? Fireball!'
jokes.setup: Dwight dramatically names his knuckles as deadly weapons in a sequence of menacing names
jokes.punchline: Kevin's pedestrian suggestion 'Smasher' is shot down — Dwight had a very specific fourth name ready: 'Fireball!' The disappointment in Dwight's tone and the absurdity of 'Fireball' for a knuckle is the payoff
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent — Kevin's intrusion and Dwight's dismissal set up 'Fireball' as the real punchline. The joke layers multiple beats: Dwight's self-seriousness, Kevin's earnest wrong answer, and 'Fireball' as an unhinged choice. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head: 'Sensei Billy says most students don't spend $150,000 over 20 years to get their black belt.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains he found a new sensei after parting with Sensei Ira, who he calls 'a bit of a shyster'
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Dwight spent $150,000 over 20 years on karate lessons — an astronomical sum delivered matter-of-factly, implying Sensei Ira milked him for decades
jokes.explanation: The specificity of $150,000 over 20 years makes this exceptional. Dwight's deadpan delivery of staggering financial self-destruction in service of karate is peak Dwight. High originality because the joke reveals a long, expensive backstory in one line. Nearly reaches the 8-anchor level.

jokes.text: Dwight announces his black belt ceremony will be 'right here in the office at lunch. Lunch not provided.'
jokes.setup: Dwight invites everyone to his black belt ceremony
jokes.punchline: 'Lunch not provided' — the bureaucratic disclaimer undercuts the grandeur of the invitation and reveals Dwight's typical office-memo mindset even in personal triumph
jokes.explanation: Three words that do enormous work. The joke is entirely in 'Lunch not provided' — Dwight's inability to separate ceremony from office logistics. Economy score nearly maxes out.

jokes.text: Dwight does a karate kick/demonstration yelling 'Fireball!' and Stanley dryly says: 'That's pretty good. I feel safe.'
jokes.setup: Dwight dramatically demonstrates his martial arts
jokes.punchline: Stanley's completely flat, insincere endorsement: 'That's pretty good. I feel safe.' — the most minimal possible acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: Classic Stanley deadpan. Works because of the contrast between Dwight's intensity and Stanley's supreme indifference. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Erin mishears 'Is Andy in?' as 'Is Indian?' and launches into: 'Is Indian food good? Is Indian jewelry pretty? Is Indian hair an expensive kind of wig? Yes to all three, by the way.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks the simple question 'Is Andy in?'
jokes.punchline: Erin's mishearing leads to an escalating list of non-sequitur 'Is Indian [X]?' questions, ending with the bizarre specificity of 'Is Indian hair an expensive kind of wig?' and a sincere 'Yes to all three'
jokes.explanation: Peak Erin. The escalation from plausible mishearing to 'Indian hair as an expensive wig' is wonderfully strange. 'Yes to all three, by the way' — her complete sincerity — sells it. Strong character integration because only Erin would go here.

jokes.text: Erin's talking-head: 'Lately, I've been having a lot of trouble keeping track of Andy's calendar. His student film audition schedule is crazy hectic.'
jokes.setup: Erin is supposed to be managing Andy's work calendar as receptionist
jokes.punchline: She instead speaks of his 'student film audition schedule' as her primary professional challenge — fully bought into Andy's delusions
jokes.explanation: Competent talking-head joke that illuminates both Andy's delusion and Erin's earnest enablement. Not exceptional but does character work efficiently.

jokes.text: 'David Walrus in his native habitat.' — Jim's aside upon seeing David Wallace
jokes.setup: Jim spots David Wallace arriving at the Scranton office
jokes.punchline: Dryly narrates his arrival as a nature documentary observation: 'David Walrus in his native habitat'
jokes.explanation: A quick Jim aside that works on economy. 'David Walrus' is a mild but functional gag. Not remarkable but earns its place.

jokes.text: David Wallace's talking-head: 'Yesterday, he asked me to pay for cheek implants. Claimed it's going to boost office morale.'
jokes.setup: Wallace is listing Andy's escalating transgressions — Caribbean trip, expensive photo printer for headshots
jokes.punchline: The final escalation: cheek implants billed as 'office morale' — the absurd justification is the joke
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation joke — the list builds (Caribbean → headshot printer → cheek implants) and each item is more absurd. 'Boost office morale' is the perfect corporate-speak fig leaf for Andy's vanity.

jokes.text: Andy explains he can't succeed because at his last headshot sitting, he was 'so distracted wondering what I was missing at work that I came across totally manic. And I was going for zany.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to explain why being at work hurts his acting career
jokes.punchline: The distinction between 'manic' and 'zany' as if they're meaningfully different target looks, and that work-distraction caused the wrong one, is perfectly delusional
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'manic' versus 'zany' as distinct headshot vibes is delicious. Only Andy would have calibrated target expressions for headshot sessions, and only Andy would treat 'came across manic' as a genuine professional setback. High character integration.

jokes.text: Andy tells David he wants to quit to pursue fame: 'I see no reason to limit myself to just acting... I am pursuing fame of any kind. Could be singing. Could be dancing. I don't... It just... I owe it to myself and my future fans.'
jokes.setup: David asks if Andy wants to quit Dunder Mifflin to pursue acting
jokes.punchline: Andy rejects the narrow framing — it's not just acting, it's 'fame of any kind' — and the kicker 'my future fans' reveals the delusional grandiosity
jokes.explanation: 'My future fans' is the knockout phrase — it reveals Andy has already mentally populated his fan base. Good character integration; this is pure delusional Andy.

jokes.text: David Wallace's talking-head after Andy quits: 'Well, that kind of worked out. I think just about anybody can be a star. My postman, the night janitor here... But Andy? No, definitely not. Charisma black hole.'
jokes.setup: Wallace is processing that Andy just quit before he could fire him
jokes.punchline: 'Charisma black hole' — delivered after generously crediting random strangers with star potential, making Andy's exclusion more devastating
jokes.explanation: 'Charisma black hole' is a genuinely great insult — novel, precise, and devastating. The structure is excellent: Wallace first generously extends star potential to nobodies, then carves Andy out specifically. The phrase 'charisma black hole' approaches quotable TV gold.

jokes.text: Jim returns to his old desk; Clark is sitting there and doesn't want to give it up: 'I've actually been working pretty hard here on a daily basis. So I kind of feel like I've earned this.' Jim: 'You totally have. You have earned it. But maybe I could be with my wife.' Clark: 'Right. Well, I'm here to sell paper.' Jim: 'Burn.'
jokes.setup: Jim asks Clark to return his old desk so he can sit near Pam
jokes.punchline: Clark's earnest comeback — 'I'm here to sell paper' — delivered as a mic drop, and Jim's begrudging 'Burn' acknowledgment of being out-argued
jokes.explanation: A funny inversion — Clark wins the argument with pure professionalism while Jim's reason (being near his wife) is sweet but loses. Jim saying 'Burn' to his own detriment is the right move.

jokes.text: Jim asks Clark: 'What do you need more face time with Wallace for? You trying to get a second second job here?'
jokes.setup: Clark wants to sit near Wallace to impress him as the new junior salesman
jokes.punchline: Jim's dig — 'a second second job' — referencing Jim's own Philly situation while implying Clark is already punching above his station
jokes.explanation: A decent self-aware joke from Jim about his own double-employment situation. Functional but not standout.

jokes.text: Jim banishes Clark to the annex, then adds: 'Be careful. It is very easy to get lost in Pete's beautiful, dead eyes.'
jokes.setup: Jim tells Clark he can sit in the annex as a consolation
jokes.punchline: The warning about Pete's 'beautiful, dead eyes' — a weirdly specific and vivid insult/compliment hybrid delivered as genuine concern
jokes.explanation: 'Beautiful, dead eyes' is a wonderfully strange phrase — it's an insult disguised as a compliment, delivered with Jim's signature deadpan concern. Good economy and originality.

jokes.text: Andy announces 'I'm taking a leave of absence from Dunder Mifflin forever.' The office starts to console him: 'It's a sad day when anybody is fired.' Andy: 'Uh-uh-uh. Andy was not fired.' Andy: 'I'm fired up. Yes.'
jokes.setup: Andy announces his departure; everyone assumes he was fired
jokes.punchline: Andy corrects them with 'I'm fired up' — a wordplay pivot that also reveals his desperate need to reframe his exit as triumphant
jokes.explanation: The 'fired/fired up' misdirection is a well-executed joke. The office's assumption that he was fired is funnier than Andy's correction, but both elements work together.

jokes.text: Phyllis's talking-head: 'Andy sings beautifully, and he's really good at dancing. He's a good speaker. But there's just something there you don't want to look at.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis is assessing Andy's chances in show business
jokes.punchline: After crediting his genuine talents, the vague but devastating 'there's just something there you don't want to look at' — an indefinable quality of off-putting-ness
jokes.explanation: A companion to Wallace's 'charisma black hole' — both identify an ineffable repellent quality. 'Something you don't want to look at' is more visceral and almost more cruel because it's less specific. The structure (compliment, compliment, devastating vague qualifier) is solid.

jokes.text: Pete to Jim: 'Hey, how am I doing as your desk mate, by the way? You probably miss Clark.' Jim: 'Yeah, a little bit.' Pete: 'Wow.' Jim: 'No, no. I get it.' Pete: 'It's cool, man. I'm sure you and I will have our own thing.' Jim: 'Yeah. Definitely. Go Phillies, right?' Pete: 'You don't watch baseball. I keep forgetting that.'
jokes.setup: Pete asks how he's doing as Jim's new desk mate, clearly hoping for validation
jokes.punchline: Jim admits he misses Clark, then tries to recover with 'Go Phillies' — which Pete knows is fake enthusiasm since Jim doesn't watch baseball
jokes.explanation: A nice awkward exchange. Jim's false enthusiasm being immediately called out ('You don't watch baseball') is a good beat. The cringe is mild but real.

jokes.text: Darryl to Andy: 'Show business is cold. Let's say you get a job, which you probably won't. They're not gonna cut you any slack. You're meant for a job with lots and lots of slack.'
jokes.setup: Darryl is trying to talk Andy out of leaving for show business
jokes.punchline: 'You're meant for a job with lots and lots of slack' — simultaneously an insult about Andy's work ethic and a genuine (if backhanded) expression of care
jokes.explanation: 'Lots and lots of slack' is well-phrased. Darryl's tough-love style is perfectly calibrated — the insult is the affection.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking-head: 'The male is a funny species. We don't just tell each other how we feel. That's chick stuff. So instead of saying, "Hey, Andy, I love you, man. I don't want you to leave," you say something like, "Hey, Andy, you're making the worst mistake of your life. You're not talented."'
jokes.setup: Darryl reflects on male communication styles in a talking-head
jokes.punchline: The translation of 'I love you, I don't want you to leave' into 'you're making the worst mistake of your life, you're not talented' — making explicit the male communication inversion
jokes.explanation: A warm, funny talking-head that contextualizes the Darryl/Andy friendship. The direct translation joke is a well-used comedy structure but executed with genuine warmth here.

jokes.text: After Darryl's sincere-in-code speech, Andy simply says: 'Right back at you, Darryl.' with full understanding, no irony.
jokes.setup: Darryl has decoded male communication as coded love-expressions
jokes.punchline: Andy receives the coded message perfectly — 'Right back at you' — meaning he loves Darryl too, within the same encoded system
jokes.explanation: Four words deliver the emotional payoff of the preceding monologue. Works because both characters are now operating in the same register. Economy is the strength — 'right back at you' is the minimum viable response and perfect for it.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking-head: 'Andy's from the generation that thinks they should all be famous. What happened to the generation that knew you shut up, did your work and died quietly from a heart attack?'
jokes.setup: Kevin is opining on Andy's career ambitions
jokes.punchline: 'Died quietly from a heart attack' — Kevin frames this as the aspirational alternative, with zero self-awareness about how bleak it sounds
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. 'Died quietly from a heart attack' as the aspirational model delivered with Kevin's total sincerity is genuinely subversive and darkly brilliant. It also has an ironic self-implicating quality — Kevin is describing himself. High originality, perfect economy, outstanding character integration. This is Kevin's finest moment and approaches the calibration anchor for 8+ jokes.

jokes.text: Kevin continues: 'Could Andy make it as an entertainer? I don't know. You know who's really funny? This bird in the park that can't fly right. I'd pay to see him. But I don't have to, 'cause the park is free.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is asked if Andy could make it as an entertainer
jokes.punchline: Kevin pivots to a bird he knows at the park, then undercuts his own willingness to pay with 'the park is free' — a perfect non-sequitur delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: A genuinely inventive joke. Kevin introduces a bird that can't fly right as a superior entertainer to Andy, then the 'but the park is free' coda is both a non-sequitur and a logical extension of Kevin's particular brand of fiscal reasoning. High originality — this is not a joke you've heard before. Matches the 8-anchor calibration.

jokes.text: Dwight's black belt ceremony: He asks Sensei Billy to take his belt and says 'I now submit to you every part of myself.' Sensei Billy replies: 'That's really okay. I'm mostly focused on the belt here.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is doing the ceremonial belt transfer with theatrical gravitas, offering his total submission
jokes.punchline: Sensei Billy's embarrassed deflection — he just wants the belt, not a full spiritual surrender
jokes.explanation: Dwight's ceremonial over-commitment vs. Sensei Billy's pragmatic awkwardness is well-executed cringe. The subversion of Dwight's gravity with Billy's matter-of-fact response works cleanly.

jokes.text: Sensei Billy: 'I can't do this if you're gonna be thrusting like that, okay? I think we're gonna have to cut this off.' The office narrator (Kevin's voice implied): 'He will now perform the ceremonial cutting off of the belt.'
jokes.setup: The belt removal ceremony has become inadvertently sexual; Billy tries to redirect
jokes.punchline: The narration deadpans 'He will now perform the ceremonial cutting off of the belt' — framing the workaround with the same pomposity as the original ceremony, implying Dwight's hip thrusts necessitated scissors
jokes.explanation: The running narration gag ('He will now perform...') combined with the awkward physicality is well-structured. The escalation from ceremony to physical cutting due to Dwight's thrusting is a strong visual comedy moment inferred from context.

jokes.text: After the thrusting makes the belt removal impossible, Billy declares: 'I think we're gonna have to cut this off.' Kevin's narrator-voice echo: 'He will now perform the ceremonial cutting off of the belt.'
jokes.setup: The belt ceremony has gone wrong; Billy proposes cutting the belt off physically
jokes.punchline: Kevin has been narrating the ceremony in a formal announcer voice; his deadpan echo of Billy's practical problem-solving as a 'ceremonial' act is the joke
jokes.explanation: Kevin elevating a logistical embarrassment to ceremonial status ('He will now perform the ceremonial cutting off of the belt') is a perfect running gag beat. The formality of the announcement against the chaos of what's happening is the joke.

jokes.text: Angela's talking-head: 'He would strap me to his chest in a Baby Bjorn made for fat children and do lunges across the farm. I felt like I was flying.'
jokes.setup: Angela is reminiscing about helping Dwight with strength training when they were dating
jokes.punchline: 'A Baby Bjorn made for fat children' — the specific product and the implications about Angela's size relative to infant gear, plus 'I felt like I was flying' delivered with sincere nostalgia
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional television comedy. 'A Baby Bjorn made for fat children' is an astonishing line — it's specific, absurd, visually hilarious, and requires no elaboration. The kicker 'I felt like I was flying' delivered with Angela's genuine wistfulness transforms it from a bizarre insult into something almost touching. High originality (this image has never existed before), perfect character integration (only Angela and Dwight's relationship could produce this memory), and the economy is flawless. Approaches the calibration anchor for 9+ material.

jokes.text: Dwight performs his kata forms while Sensei Billy spectates. Dwight keeps checking: 'Sensei, you're not watching.' Billy: 'Yeah, I'm watching.' 'Watch this part, okay?' followed by Billy's visible disengagement
jokes.setup: Dwight performs his final kata forms, desperate for Billy's approval
jokes.punchline: Billy's obvious inattention contrasted with Dwight's needy performance — the visual of a black belt recipient performing for an uninterested sensei
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Dwight's need for validation vs. Billy's complete indifference. A solid repeated bit but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Sensei, do you generally do house calls like this?' Billy: 'You can just call me Billy. And no. No, but Dwight insisted. He wanted to receive his black belt in the place he loves most in the world. He said that?' [Billy nods] 'He's an odd guy, isn't he?' 'Yes.' 'Irritating? Also yes.'
jokes.setup: Jim learns Dwight specifically requested to receive his belt at the office — the place he loves most
jokes.punchline: Jim's rapid-fire 'He's an odd guy?' / 'Irritating? Also yes.' exchange with Billy — bonding over Dwight with understated efficiency
jokes.explanation: Two layers working simultaneously: the sweet reveal that Dwight loves the office most in the world, and Jim and Billy immediately bonding as mutual Dwight sufferers. The 'Irritating? Also yes' structure (offering the descriptor then confirming it) is a nice joke construction.

jokes.text: Kevin and Toby confront Andy with a list of objections to quitting: '...in your late 30s with no savings to fall back on and no real connections in that business, which can be competitive. Yeah, sure. What's your question?' 'Our question is... it seems dumb.'
jokes.setup: Kevin and Toby build an elaborate, specific case against Andy quitting — late 30s, no savings, no connections — framed as leading to a question
jokes.punchline: 'Our question is... it seems dumb.' — the entire preamble was just building to a non-question statement
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. The long windup to 'it seems dumb' is a perfect anti-climax — they literally set up a question format and then just delivered a verdict. The structure does the heavy lifting and it lands well.

jokes.text: Toby proposes Andy stay and 'full-ass' it as manager. Kevin: 'Really give it a go? Be the greatest manager in the history of this branch and in that way, achieve the fame and immortality that you seek?'
jokes.setup: Toby and Kevin try to convince Andy that staying as manager could fulfill his need for fame
jokes.punchline: Kevin escalates the pitch to 'fame and immortality' — going way further than office management could plausibly deliver, with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Decent bit but a little elongated. The 'fame and immortality' escalation is funny but the sequence runs slightly long.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Nobody is going to hire you ever. You're too character-y to be a lead, and you're not fat enough to be a great character actor.'
jokes.setup: Andy rejects the manager pitch; Toby drops the diplomatic approach
jokes.punchline: The precise industry analysis: too character-y for leads, not fat enough for character work — a specific, credible Hollywood catch-22 that's also devastating
jokes.explanation: This is a great joke. 'Too character-y to be a lead, not fat enough to be a great character actor' is specific, rings true as Hollywood logic, and is uniquely devastating because it's not a generic insult — it's a precise, credible industry assessment. Economy is high. Approaches the 8-anchor calibration cleanly.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking-head: 'No, I don't think he can make it as an actor. But he also can't make it as an employee in an office, so, you know, why not go nuts with it?'
jokes.setup: Kevin assesses Andy's chances
jokes.punchline: 'Why not go nuts with it?' — Kevin's fatalistic endorsement of Andy's dream based purely on Andy's complete incompetence everywhere else
jokes.explanation: Kevin's logic is perfect — Andy failing everywhere means entertainment is as good a place as any. The endorsement-as-insult structure is well executed and very Kevin.

jokes.text: Dwight and Jim interact over office supplies. Dwight: 'If you want to get rid of a headache, you sit on something sharp. Any sensei will tell you that.'
jokes.setup: Jim mentions aspirin for a headache; Dwight offers his sensei-endorsed alternative
jokes.punchline: 'You sit on something sharp. Any sensei will tell you that.' — presented as received martial wisdom
jokes.explanation: The false authority of 'any sensei will tell you that' elevates what is essentially absurd folk wisdom. Dwight's confident delivery of this as medical fact is perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Wallace to Dwight: 'I've been considering you for manager. Am I crazy?' Jim: 'Not at all. It should be Dwight.' Wallace: 'You sure?' Jim: 'You're going to want to invest in a lot more liability insurance, but... Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Wallace asks Jim if making Dwight manager is a good idea
jokes.punchline: Jim's endorsement comes with the caveat of significantly increased liability insurance — an acknowledgment of Dwight's danger without taking back the endorsement
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'liability insurance' qualifier is a precise, knowing joke about Dwight's history of workplace dangers. Well-calibrated endorsement-as-warning.

jokes.text: Wallace tells Andy his plan 'seems dumb,' Andy fires back with 'it's better than sticking around here and half-assing it.' Toby: 'But what if you were to stay here and "full-ass" it?'
jokes.setup: Andy uses 'half-assing it' as a defense
jokes.punchline: Toby earnestly adopts the 'half-ass/full-ass' vocabulary as a legitimate counterargument — 'full-ass it'
jokes.explanation: 'Full-ass it' works because Toby's sincerity transforms the crass vocabulary into earnest professional advice. The character-appropriateness of Toby making this case is good.

jokes.text: Wallace tells Andy he has nothing to gain from Andy staying but: 'Dear God, don't quit your dayjob.' Then: 'Nothing is impossible to him who will try. Alexander the Great, if he were Cockney.' Andy: 'You're bad.' Wallace: 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Wallace is giving Andy an honest assessment mixed with dark encouragement
jokes.punchline: Wallace does a Cockney accent approximation of Alexander the Great's quote, then Andy calls him out — 'You're bad' — which Wallace accepts with casual pride
jokes.explanation: A fun unexpected bit from Wallace — the Cockney Alexander impression is absurd and the rapport between him and Andy in this moment is charming. Not exceptional but enjoyable.

jokes.text: Wallace quotes: 'Nothing is impossible to him who will try. Alexander the Great, if he were Cockney.'
jokes.setup: Andy delivers a quote to justify his decision; Wallace responds
jokes.punchline: The attribution — 'Alexander the Great, if he were Cockney' — reframes the quote as a dialect joke, suggesting the grammar ('him who will try') sounds Cockney
jokes.explanation: A sharp, unexpected comedy choice. The specific observation that the grammar of the quote sounds Cockney is original — it's a linguistic/absurdist joke that most writers wouldn't think of. Wallace's deadpan delivery of 'if he were Cockney' is a highlight of his character's dry wit.

jokes.text: Andy to Erin: 'Honest Erin. Cannot tell a lie. We lay together. That's something you can't take back.' Erin: 'So true.'
jokes.setup: Andy appeals to Erin for her honest opinion, invoking their history as ex-lovers
jokes.punchline: 'We lay together. That's something you can't take back.' Erin's sincere 'So true' — both characters treating this as a neutral credential-establishing fact
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'we lay together' as a matter-of-fact honesty credential is slightly odd in a funny way. Both characters' unironic treatment of their history is good cringe.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm gonna make it. Every person who's been on Conan has a crazy story about how they made it. Every person.'
jokes.setup: Andy is presenting his evidence that long shots can succeed
jokes.punchline: Using 'every person who's been on Conan' as the population set for success stories — as if Conan guests are a comprehensive sample of all successful people — is delusionally narrow logic
jokes.explanation: Andy's faulty logic is character-consistent. The specificity of 'Conan' rather than a generic talk show adds a comic texture. Works as a character beat, not a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Erin tells Andy bluntly: 'Yes. Huge mistake. Andy, honestly, I think you might become homeless or maybe even starve.' Andy: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Erin to tell him bluntly if he's making a mistake
jokes.punchline: Erin's prediction of homelessness and starvation, followed by Andy's sincere 'Thank you' — he asked for bluntness and is oddly grateful for the dire prediction
jokes.explanation: Erin's sincerity in predicting Andy's doom is funny on its own, but Andy's grateful 'Thank you' adds a layer — he needed to hear the worst to feel validated in his rebellion. Good character work from both.

jokes.text: Dwight enters Wallace's office. Wallace: 'Will you be the new manager?' Dwight: 'Where? What branch? Here. Scranton.' Dwight collapses to the floor overcome with emotion.
jokes.setup: Dwight is called into Wallace's office, not knowing what to expect
jokes.punchline: Dwight's complete emotional collapse on the floor upon learning he's manager — the man who has wanted this his entire career literally cannot stand
jokes.explanation: The physical collapse is earned — nine seasons of Dwight wanting to be manager pay off here. The comedy comes from the extreme physical expression of genuine emotion. 'Come on, Dwight. Get up. Let's go. It's good news.' from Wallace is the right deadpan accompaniment.

jokes.text: Dwight is told he'll be manager. After a long pause, almost in tears: 'I've just waited for this moment my entire life. I mean, I was interim manager once, but then I shot that gun.'
jokes.setup: David Wallace formally offers Dwight the manager position
jokes.punchline: 'I was interim manager once, but then I shot that gun' — the matter-of-fact callback to a specific past failure, dropped into an emotional moment, is a perfect comedy/pathos beat
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed joke that works on multiple levels: the emotional sincerity of the moment, the callback to a specific (and absurd) past event, and the understatement of 'but then I shot that gun' as the simple explanation for failure. It's earned by seasons of character development. The sentence structure — interrupting genuine emotion with a practical, shameless aside — is perfect. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Dwight pulls out a pre-made 'Dwight K. Schrute — Manager' plaque/nameplate. Wallace: 'Why do you already have this?' Dwight: 'In case Michael or Andy ever got killed in a traffic accident and there was a trade show on the same day.'
jokes.setup: Dwight produces a managerial nameplate that he apparently prepared in advance
jokes.punchline: The specific scenario he'd prepared for: both previous managers dying in a traffic accident while a trade show was happening simultaneously — the specificity of 'traffic accident AND trade show same day' reveals years of contingency planning
jokes.explanation: Elite Office joke. The specificity of 'killed in a traffic accident and there was a trade show on the same day' is the key — Dwight has not only dreamed of being manager but has war-gamed the exact dual-catastrophe scenario that would require him to step up, and prepared accordingly. The 'AND a trade show' qualifier reveals a deeply Dwight logic: it wasn't just the deaths that would matter, it was the professional necessity. Near-perfect character integration. Approaches the 9+ calibration range.

jokes.text: Jim goes to Pam's desk with a fake 'question' — their entire interaction is a romantic dance of pretending he didn't just come back for her
jokes.setup: Jim approaches Pam saying he has a question — it becomes clear he has no question and just came to see her
jokes.punchline: 'I did not come back here just to see you.' / 'No, I'm sure you did not.' / 'What was your question?' / 'I don't know, but it might take me a long time to figure it out.'
jokes.explanation: The Jim/Pam romantic banter is warm and well-executed. 'It might take me a long time to figure it out' is sweet and funny — Jim's transparent ruse being played straight by both of them. It's not the sharpest writing in the episode but it's emotionally resonant and characteristically theirs.

jokes.text: Andy returns having changed his mind again: 'Hey, everybody. I changed my mind. Not leaving. I'm gonna stay on in sales.' Kevin: 'Oh! Thank God!' then immediately: 'Because sales could be your best role yet.'
jokes.setup: Andy reverses his decision to leave
jokes.punchline: Kevin's instant pivot from apparent relief to framing sales as a 'role' — he can't stop thinking in acting terms even when trying to be supportive
jokes.explanation: Functional joke, good quick beat. Kevin's accidental validation of the actor framing is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'Don't wanna see you in a porn next year.'
jokes.setup: The office is receiving Andy's decision to stay
jokes.punchline: Darryl's specific fear is that Andy would end up in pornography — delivered as a genuine expression of concern/relief
jokes.explanation: Quick, effective dark joke. The economy is good; the specificity of 'porn next year' as Darryl's concern is funny. Slightly cheap but earns the laugh.

jokes.text: Oscar suggests Andy stay and embrace 'Death of a Salesman.' Andy: 'I don't think so.' Oscar: 'Sure, Death of a Salesman by Arthur Miller. It's a great play about crushed dreams.' Andy: 'No, this one was written by SpongeBob SquarePants.'
jokes.setup: Oscar recommends 'Death of a Salesman' as relevant to Andy's situation
jokes.punchline: Andy's alternate attribution: 'This one was written by SpongeBob SquarePants' — delivered with total confidence, suggesting Andy has encountered a completely different 'Death of a Salesman'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great joke. The confidence with which Andy attributes 'Death of a Salesman' to SpongeBob SquarePants implies he has some parallel cultural reference he's confusing with Arthur Miller — and he's completely certain. The absurdity is pure Andy: privileged, confused, unshakeable. High originality, excellent character integration, good economy.

jokes.text: Jim demonstrates reverse stapling to Dwight: 'The staple crimps outward.' Dwight: 'And here I've been stapling the same way for 20 years like a frickin' sheep.'
jokes.setup: Jim shows Dwight a stapling trick
jokes.punchline: Dwight's self-flagellating 'like a frickin' sheep' — the intensity of his shame about a minor technique is pure Dwight
jokes.explanation: A sweet Jim-Dwight bonding moment played as comedy. 'Like a frickin' sheep' is a characteristically over-intense Dwight response to a minor revelation.

jokes.text: Jim and Dwight banter about a double date with Pete and his girlfriend. When Thursday is suggested, both Jim and Dwight immediately cite scheduling conflicts. 'Just forget it. Forget I said anything.' Jim stares at camera. [Awkward silence]
jokes.setup: Pete naively suggests a double date; Jim and Dwight both deflect
jokes.punchline: The collective backpedaling and Jim's camera look — the audience understands Jim and Dwight would never actually want to double-date with Pete and his girlfriend
jokes.explanation: A classic Office awkward beat. The camera look from Jim is the payoff. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dwight's phone rings during Wallace's announcement. Dwight: 'Can I just do one thing while you're making this announcement? And then I'll never, ever do it again.' Wallace: 'I don't think so.' Dwight: 'It's just one thing. Just let me...' [sends phone to voicemail, clearly reluctantly]
jokes.setup: Wallace is about to announce Dwight as the new manager
jokes.punchline: Dwight's inability to ignore a ringing phone even in his greatest professional moment — he literally needs permission and still can't fully let go
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Dwight's professionalism compulsion interfering with his biggest moment. The 'I'll never, ever do it again' implies this is a recurring battle for him.

jokes.text: Dwight calls his uncle on speakerphone: 'Then we'll get him a new set of drums.' [clearly mid-conversation about something totally mundane before Dwight hangs up and announces himself as manager]
jokes.setup: Dwight makes a phone call before his big announcement — we expect it to be important
jokes.punchline: The call is to his uncle about getting someone new drums — a completely mundane conversation that has nothing to do with the moment, suggesting Dwight called to share his news and the uncle pivoted to drums
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a new set of drums' as the fragment of conversation we hear is perfectly Schrute-world absurdist. The family moves quickly past Dwight's biggest news to discuss percussion instruments.

jokes.text: Creed Bratton upon Dwight's announcement: 'Creed Bratton is the new manager!'
jokes.setup: Dwight is announced as the new manager; the office celebrates
jokes.punchline: Creed announces himself as the new manager — apparently mishearing or choosing to insert himself into the announcement
jokes.explanation: Pure Creed. The joke requires no setup beyond knowing Creed always believes he's the protagonist of his own reality. Maximum economy. Strong character integration — this line could only work from Creed.

jokes.text: Dwight tells Clark to get out of Jim's chair: 'You're an annex kid. You might be bullpen. We'll see. Give it a couple years. Scram.'
jokes.setup: Dwight, as new manager, begins asserting authority
jokes.punchline: The hierarchy Dwight immediately establishes (annex kid → maybe bullpen → years away) and the dismissive 'Scram' — his first managerial act is seating classification
jokes.explanation: Dwight's first act as manager is exactly what you'd expect: creating a caste system with himself as arbiter. 'Annex kid' as an identity category and 'Scram' as a managerial directive is perfectly Dwight.

jokes.text: Wallace offers Jim 'assistant regional manager.' Jim: 'Nope. Can't accept that job. It's not a real job.' Jim: 'I'll tell you what I could accept is assistant to the regional manager. That is a real job, and one I'd be proud to take.' Wallace: 'Shake on it?' Jim: 'Done. Way to negotiate, idiot.'
jokes.setup: Wallace offers Jim a promotion to assistant regional manager
jokes.punchline: Jim negotiates himself down to 'assistant TO the regional manager' — Dwight's old title — and congratulates himself sarcastically: 'Way to negotiate, idiot'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most structurally sophisticated joke and one of the great callbacks in the series. Jim knowingly negotiates himself into Dwight's old title — the title he spent years mocking — and then immediately recognizes the absurdity with 'Way to negotiate, idiot.' The joke works on multiple levels: the long-running gag payoff, Jim's self-awareness, the sweetness of him wanting to be Dwight's right hand, and the self-deprecating punchline. Near the calibration ceiling for craft.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head: 'When Cortés landed in Mexico, the only way he got his men to defeat the Aztecs was by burning all of his own boats so they could never return home. Huge dick move, but very effective. I need to be that same kind of dick to myself.'
jokes.setup: Andy is processing how quickly he abandoned his dream when given a fallback
jokes.punchline: 'Huge dick move, but very effective. I need to be that same kind of dick to myself.' — Andy's historical analysis ends in self-directed profanity as motivation
jokes.explanation: 'Huge dick move, but very effective' as a pivot from historical analysis to self-motivation is genuinely funny. 'I need to be that same kind of dick to myself' recontextualizes the metaphor in a perfectly Andy way. Good structure — builds to the punchline naturally.

jokes.text: Andy changes his mind AGAIN and announces he's going with his dream — 'Gotta go all in. Ain't that right, Jim?' Jim: 'Oh. Don't look at me, 'cause I think you're making a terrible choice.' Andy: 'All in! Whoo!'
jokes.setup: Andy has just re-changed his mind AGAIN to leave, citing the Cortés metaphor
jokes.punchline: Andy tries to get Jim's endorsement for 'going all in' — Jim explicitly refuses and says it's a terrible choice — Andy ignores this and shouts 'All in! Whoo!' anyway
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Andy changing his mind has good escalation — this is now the third change. Jim refusing to endorse it while Andy ignores him is a good character dynamic moment. The 'All in! Whoo!' is committing energy.

jokes.text: Andy asks Toby to put in his file that he was 'fired for theft and/or groping wieners.' Toby refuses. Andy: 'Just know that you made me do this.' [Andy proceeds to grope Toby] Toby: 'Come on. Andy, no. God, Toby, don't... Stop blocking my hand.' Andy: 'Groped you good. Off to Hollywood!'
jokes.setup: Andy wants his file to say he was fired for misconduct so he can't fall back on Dunder Mifflin
jokes.punchline: When Toby won't lie for him, Andy manufactures the misconduct in real time by actually groping Toby, declaring 'Groped you good. Off to Hollywood!'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'put it in my file' to actually committing the act is a great logical joke — Andy's willingness to cause real misconduct to avoid having fictional misconduct documented is wonderfully perverse. 'Groped you good' is a genuinely funny line. High character integration for both: Andy's dramatic self-destruction and Toby's helpless victimhood.

jokes.text: Angela is on the phone, apparently with her landlord. She pivots from defending herself about rent to hearing she's been evicted, ending with: 'You have so many hairs on your chin, Animal Control should've taken you away.'
jokes.setup: Angela confidently answers what she thinks is a rent issue call
jokes.punchline: The escalation to eviction and Angela's furious parting insult — 'Animal Control should've taken you away' — reappropriating the animal control theme from her own cat situation as a weapon
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Animal Control cat removal as an insult weapon is clever and character-perfect. Angela's fury and the specificity of the chin-hair detail is good. The structural irony of Animal Control being turned back on the landlord is satisfying.

jokes.text: Andy is trying to get fired by confessing to losing the Scranton White Pages account: 'I did it out of spite.' Wallace: 'We put the past behind us, Andy.' Andy: 'What if I told you I hate you and this company?' Wallace: 'Enough, Andy. Enough!' Andy: 'Just stop forgiving me, David. Please?'
jokes.setup: Andy is desperately trying to get himself fired so Dunder Mifflin isn't a fallback
jokes.punchline: 'Just stop forgiving me, David. Please?' — Andy's exasperated plea for Wallace to stop being reasonable
jokes.explanation: 'Just stop forgiving me, David. Please?' is an outstanding line — the desperation of someone begging their boss to stop being magnanimous is a genuinely original comic premise. Wallace's implacable forgiveness as the obstacle is a great structural inversion.

jokes.text: Andy threatens: 'What if I took a dump on your new car?' Then quotes Eleanor Roosevelt: 'The future belongs to those who believe in the beauty of their dreams.' Wallace: 'Get out!'
jokes.setup: Andy is escalating his attempts to get fired
jokes.punchline: The whiplash from threatening to defecate on Wallace's car to immediately quoting Eleanor Roosevelt as a non-sequitur — the juxtaposition is the joke
jokes.explanation: The Eleanor Roosevelt pivot after the car threat is a good tonal whiplash. Andy's sincere framing of it all ('I feel calm now') adds to the comedy. Not exceptional but well-executed absurdism.

jokes.text: Pam catches Andy packing: 'What are you doing?' Andy: 'Heavy stuff like books on the bottom. So I don't squash my knickety-knacks on top.'
jokes.setup: Pam catches Andy in the middle of packing up his office
jokes.punchline: 'My knickety-knacks' — Andy's casual inventory term for his office trinkets, delivered as if this is normal packing advice
jokes.explanation: 'Knickety-knacks' is a slightly funny word choice but this is a mild joke. Functional scene-setting comedy.

jokes.text: Andy misreads Angela's speech about not rehashing the past as being about their romantic history: 'What we had was great, and honestly I think about it a lot, too.' Angela recoils in confusion.
jokes.setup: Angela is giving Andy sincere advice about not letting pride ruin his life
jokes.punchline: Andy completely misreads the conversation as being about their brief romantic history and responds with nostalgic warmth, while Angela is bewildered
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe misdirection. Andy's self-centered reading of Angela's advice as romance-related is in character and produces a good awkward exchange.

jokes.text: Angela watches Andy leave and says quietly: 'A bridge a-burnt. No turning back now.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just awkwardly invoked their romantic history and left
jokes.punchline: Angela's dryly poetic 'A bridge a-burnt' — delivering a slightly mangled idiom as solemn commentary on a moment that was already weird
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — 'a bridge a-burnt' as a slightly poetic inversion is gentle wordplay. Works as a character moment more than a laugh line.

jokes.text: Andy announces his goodbye: 'Everybody, Lorelei and I would like to say thank you and goodbye the only way we know how.' Someone: 'Good lord.' Another: 'Can't you just leave?'
jokes.setup: Andy prepares a musical goodbye performance with his guitar (named Lorelei)
jokes.punchline: The office's immediate dread — 'Good lord,' 'Can't you just leave?' — before Andy even begins performing
jokes.explanation: The office's preemptive dread of Andy's performance is funny. 'Can't you just leave?' as a reaction to a sentimental gesture is a good tonal punch.

jokes.text: After Andy's performance, Kevin and Oscar debate his potential: Kevin: 'He's not terrible. Yeah. And people worse than him make it all the time, like Lil' Romeo.' Oscar: 'No, he's good.' Kevin: 'He was good.'
jokes.setup: The office is processing Andy's goodbye performance
jokes.punchline: Kevin's mild endorsement qualified with Lil' Romeo as a 'worse' success story, then the correction: Oscar says Lil' Romeo is 'good,' Kevin revises to past tense: 'He was good.'
jokes.explanation: The 'is/was good' correction is a nice subtle dig at Lil' Romeo's career trajectory. Kevin's instinct to use him as a floor-level comparison is funny, and Oscar's correction produces a decent additional beat.

jokes.text: Kevin and Oscar goodnight exchange — 'Good night, Kevin.' 'Night, Oscar.' — a quiet, warm beat that plays as comedy through its mundane sweetness after the emotional Andy sequence.
jokes.setup: The office empties after Andy's performance; Kevin and Oscar are the last to leave
jokes.punchline: The completeness of the ordinary exchange — just 'Good night' — as a comedy/emotional button
jokes.explanation: More of a warm button than a joke. Works emotionally but doesn't have comedic craft to score high. Included for completeness — it gets a small smile but not a laugh.

jokes.text: Oscar finds Angela looking at tents in a catalog. 'Tents? Are you thinking of going camping? I thought you found nature vulgar.' Angela: 'Well, I've changed my mind.' Oscar: 'Wait a minute, Angela. You're not thinking of living in a tent...' Angela: 'God, would you just mind your own business?'
jokes.setup: Oscar notices Angela browsing camping gear — an out-of-character interest
jokes.punchline: The dawning realization that Angela, having been evicted, is considering tent living — and her defensive 'mind your own business' confirms it
jokes.explanation: A dark payoff to the eviction storyline. The juxtaposition of Angela's snobbery ('nature is vulgar') with genuine tent consideration is a strong character-comedy beat. The implication is appropriately grim.

jokes.text: Oscar invites Angela to stay with him. Angela: 'Separate bathrooms.' Then a long beat. Angela: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Oscar offers Angela his home
jokes.punchline: Angela's first instinct is not gratitude but negotiating terms: 'Separate bathrooms.' The beat before 'Thank you' suggests she's waiting to see if Oscar will agree before thanking him
jokes.explanation: Two words do everything. 'Separate bathrooms' as Angela's first response to an act of charity perfectly encapsulates her character — the conditions precede the gratitude, and the conditions are non-negotiable. The pause before 'Thank you' implies it's conditional on the bathroom agreement. Excellent economy and the highest possible character integration. Among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Oscar asks if he's allowed to have pets. 'Oh, Angela.' — the implication being that this is obviously going to cause trouble.
jokes.setup: Oscar and Angela are making arrangements for her to move in
jokes.punchline: Oscar's doomed question about pets — and Angela's non-answer answered by his own resigned 'Oh, Angela' — implies the cat situation is about to become Oscar's problem
jokes.explanation: A good implied callback to the cat situation. Oscar's dawning horror — 'Oh, Angela' — is a nice button that promises future comedic consequences. Works as a scene-closer.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Are you allowed to have pets?' [beat] Angela's expression. Oscar: 'Oh, Angela.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is making plans to take Angela in
jokes.punchline: The question about pets — knowing Angela just lost a studio apartment's worth of cats — and Oscar's 'Oh, Angela' when the answer is clearly yes, she will try to bring cats
jokes.explanation: Efficient callback. 'Oh, Angela' landing as the punchline after the pets question implies Angela's expression confirms exactly what Oscar feared. The economy is excellent and it closes the cat storyline with a perfect button.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head: 'Yesterday, I was just your average, ordinary paper salesman with a farm and a bunch of pipe dreams about beet fuel. Today, I leave here a regional manager with a black belt. It really is amazing how your life can change in one day.'
jokes.setup: Dwight reflects on the transformative events of the day
jokes.punchline: 'A farm and a bunch of pipe dreams about beet fuel' — Dwight's self-description as 'average and ordinary' while mentioning beet fuel as a normal aspiration is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Pipe dreams about beet fuel' as Dwight's version of average-person aspirations is perfectly character-integrated. The sincerity with which he describes himself as 'ordinary' while listing the beet fuel dreams is the joke — Dwight has no idea how specific his worldview is.

jokes.text: Jim hears the Athlead offer: they want to pitch across the whole country — three months. Jim: 'Yeah, I can't do it.' His partners: 'Can't do what?' Jim: 'This, man. I can't do this to Pam.'
jokes.setup: Jim's Athlead partners call with a massive expansion opportunity — everything they've been working toward
jokes.punchline: Jim turns it down immediately, without deliberation — 'I can't do this to Pam' — a punchline in the sense that the entire Philly storyline ends in one quiet sentence
jokes.explanation: This is more emotional than comedic but qualifies as character comedy — the joke is that Jim's answer is immediate and total, no deliberation whatsoever. The comedy is in the speed and finality of his decision. Works as a warm moment more than a laugh line but the swift resolution has a comedic quality.

jokes.text: Angela moves into Oscar's apartment. Oscar: 'So is your place all bachelor, slobby and gross?' Oscar: 'Nope, it's neat and tastefully appointed, like most gay men's homes. The stereotype holds up.' Angela: 'I wouldn't know. I never lived with a gay guy.' [beat] Oscar: 'Angela, you just were...' [Long pause. Angela realizes.]
jokes.setup: Angela claims she's never lived with a gay man — apparently forgetting her husband, the Senator, who was gay
jokes.punchline: Oscar's gentle 'Angela, you just were...' and the implied dawning realization — Angela lived with a closeted gay man and apparently hasn't fully processed this
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke. Angela's casual erasure of her entire marriage — 'I never lived with a gay guy' — when she literally just did, is perfect character comedy. Oscar's gentle correction and the implied beat where reality lands is excellent structure. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: Angela, after a long pause, quietly: 'I love him.' Oscar: 'I know. I understand more than most, but we both have to move on.' Angela: 'No, not the Senator. I love Dwight.'
jokes.setup: Oscar seems to think Angela is confessing lingering feelings for the Senator
jokes.punchline: 'No, not the Senator. I love Dwight.' — the clarification reveals Angela's heart has been with Dwight all along, recontextualizing the entire conversation
jokes.explanation: A genuinely moving and funny moment simultaneously — the best kind of Office ending beat. The misdirection (we think she means the Senator) followed by 'No, not the Senator. I love Dwight.' is both a punchline and an emotional payoff. The economy is perfect — six words undo all the confusion. High structure, high character integration. The joke IS the revelation.

tmdb_overview: Dwight becomes regional manager after Andy quits his job, Jim dedicates more time to his Dunder Mifflin job to save his marriage, and Angela has problems with her new living arrangements after her breakup with The Senator.
